title: Intro to multi-agent systems and frameworks
notes: When one agent has too many tools or jobs, split the work into specialist agents with a coordinator that routes each request.
More agents mean more model calls, more cost and more places to break, so start with one and split only when tests show it struggling.
Frameworks and SDKs such as Anthropic's tool runner, LangGraph, CrewAI or a managed agent platform give you the loop, tools and memory ready-made.

slides.title: Intro to multi-agent systems and frameworks
slides.sub: When one agent is not enough, and what frameworks do for you
sentences: Scout is one agent with six tools, and that is the right size for Orbit today.
But Maya already has plans: wholesale orders for outdoor shops, and help for Sam with stock.
In this lesson you will learn when to split work across several agents, what that costs, and what frameworks can do for you.

slides.title: When one agent gets crowded
slides.scenario: Maya wants Scout to handle wholesale orders too: about ten new tools, trade prices and a second set of rules.

steps.text: 6 tools, one policy. Scout picks the right tool almost every time.
16 tools, two price lists and two sets of rules in one prompt.
Scout quotes a trade price to a retail customer.
Every request pays for 16 tool definitions, even the simple ones.

result.text: Too many tools and jobs in one prompt: more mix-ups, more tokens, harder to test.

sentences: Picture what happens if Scout simply keeps growing.
Today Scout has six tools, all about retail support, and it picks the right one almost every time.
Now add wholesale: ten more tools, a trade price list and a second set of rules, all in the same prompt.
The model now has more ways to go wrong, such as quoting a trade price to a retail customer.
And every request pays for sixteen tool definitions, even a simple question about where an order is.
When one agent juggles too many tools and jobs, mistakes go up, cost goes up and testing gets harder.

slides.title: Specialists with a coordinator

note.text: Each specialist has a short prompt and only the tools its job needs.

sentences: The usual answer is to split the work between specialists, with a coordinator in front.
Scout stays the retail specialist, with its six tools and the retail policy.
A wholesale agent gets its own prompt, its own tools and its own price list.
Later, a stock agent could help Sam plan reorders from the warehouse sheet.
The coordinator reads each request and passes it to the right specialist; it can be as simple as the ticket classifier you built in Module 2.
Each specialist stays small, so it is easier to prompt, cheaper to run and easier to test on its own.

slides.title: One request through the team

note.text: Agents pass short summaries to each other, not whole conversations. Less to read, less to pay for.

sentences: Here is one request moving through the team.
A shop owner asks for forty green two person tents for their store.
The coordinator classifies it as wholesale and passes a short summary to the wholesale agent.
The wholesale agent checks stock and finds only four of those tents in the warehouse.
It replies honestly with what is available and hands the rest of the order to Maya to confirm.
Notice that agents pass short summaries to each other rather than whole conversations, which keeps every call small.

slides.title: One agent or several?

left.label: One agent
points: One prompt and one loop to test
Mixes up jobs as tools pile up

right.label: Several agents
points: Extra calls to route and hand over
More places to break and to trace
Worth it when one agent clearly struggles

sentences: Splitting is not free, so weigh it honestly.
One agent means one prompt and one loop to test, and the fewest model calls per answer.
Its weakness is crowding: as tools and jobs pile up, it starts to mix them up.
Several agents get small, focused prompts, but every request now pays for extra calls to route it and hand it over.
There are also more places to break, and one customer's trace now spans several agents, so debugging takes longer.
The rule of thumb: start with one agent, measure it, and split only when your tests show it struggling.

slides.title: Frameworks give you the loop

cards.title: Anthropic tool runner
flow: Runs the tool loop for you

sentences: You built Scout's loop by hand, and that was on purpose.
Frameworks and SDKs give you the loop, the tool plumbing and often memory, ready-made.
Anthropic's Python SDK has a tool runner: you write the tool functions, and it runs the loop for you.
Open-source frameworks such as LangGraph and CrewAI go further, wiring several agents into graphs or teams, and they work with many model providers.
Managed agent platforms go furthest, running the loop, the tools and the memory on the provider's own servers.
Each step up means less code to write, and less control over what happens inside.

slides.title: Why you built it by hand first
slides.lead: Every framework does the same few jobs you have now written yourself.

bullets.text: The tool loop: call the model, run tools, send results back
Memory: what to keep, what to trim
Guardrails: step limits, spend limits and approvals
Debugging: reading a trace one step at a time

aside.label: When a framework surprises you
aside.text: You know what it must be doing inside, so you know where to look.

sentences: So why build the loop yourself first?
Because every framework does the same few jobs you have now written by hand, starting with the tool loop.
It manages memory, deciding what to keep in the conversation and what to trim.
It needs the same guardrails, so you still check that a step limit and a spend limit are really set.
And when something goes wrong, you read its trace one step at a time, just as you did in Module 5.
Because you understand what happens inside, a framework becomes a time saver instead of a mystery.

slides.title: Recap: multi-agent systems and frameworks

points.text: Split into specialists when one agent has too many tools or jobs.
A coordinator routes each request; agents pass short summaries.
More agents mean more calls, cost and debugging. Start with one.
Frameworks supply the loop, tools and memory; you know what they do.

sentences: Let us recap.
When one agent has too many tools or jobs, split it into specialists, each with a short prompt and its own tools.
A coordinator routes each request, and agents pass short summaries rather than whole conversations.
More agents mean more calls, more cost and more to debug, so start with one and split only when tests show you must.
Frameworks and managed platforms give you the loop, tools and memory ready-made, and now you know what they do inside.

midQuiz.q: Which sign suggests Scout should be split into specialist agents?
options: Scout takes three steps to answer a tracking question
After ten wholesale tools were added, Scout mixes up retail and trade prices
Scout's daily cost doubled because ticket volume doubled
midQuiz.explain: Mixing up two jobs after the prompt and tool list grew is the classic sign of a crowded agent. Three steps is normal, and cost that tracks volume is expected.
midQuiz.hint: Look for the option where one agent is doing two different jobs badly.

midQuiz.q: What does the coordinator do in a multi-agent setup?
options: Runs every tool itself, then asks the specialists to check
Reads each request and passes it to the right specialist
Stores the full conversation history for all the agents
midQuiz.explain: The coordinator routes. It can be as simple as a classifier that reads the intent and passes a short summary to the right specialist.
midQuiz.hint: Think of a receptionist, not a manager who does everyone's work.

endQuiz.q: What is the main cost of moving from one agent to several?
options: Extra model calls, and more places to break and debug
The agents can no longer use tools
Each agent needs its own separate API key
endQuiz.explain: Routing and hand-overs add model calls, and a problem can now hide in any agent or between them. That is why you split only when one agent clearly struggles.
endQuiz.hint: What happens to the number of model calls, and to the trace, when work is passed between agents?

endQuiz.q: Why did this course have you write the tool loop by hand before using a framework?
options: Frameworks are too slow for real agents
So you understand what a framework does inside, and can debug it
Because frameworks cannot use custom tools
endQuiz.explain: Frameworks run the same loop, memory and guardrails you built. Knowing them from the inside means a framework saves you time instead of hiding problems.
endQuiz.hint: Think about the moment a framework does something you did not expect.
